title: Thinking Like a Physicist
learning_target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.
i_can_statements: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating an inference as an observation
assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible
treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning
modeling_application_opportunities: connect a simple relationship to the quantities it represents
conceptual_anchor_headings: How Eratosthenes Measured the Size of Earth

title: Forces and Newton’s First Law
learning_target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.
i_can_statements: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.
I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.
misconceptions_failure_points: Calling inertia a force
assuming motion requires a net forward force
confusing no force with zero net force
modeling_application_opportunities: and moving vehicles to predict whether motion should remain unchanged or change

title: Net Force and Vectors
learning_target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.
i_can_statements: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.
misconceptions_failure_points: Adding vector magnitudes without direction
treating arrow length as decorative
reversing resultant direction
modeling_application_opportunities: and connect resultant direction to expected motion change

title: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion
learning_target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.
i_can_statements: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.
misconceptions_failure_points: Equating equilibrium with rest only
assuming constant speed always means equilibrium when direction changes
assuming forces disappear at equilibrium
modeling_application_opportunities: defend whether the system is in equilibrium

title: Modeling Forces in the Real World
learning_target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.
i_can_statements: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.
misconceptions_failure_points: Including forces that act on other objects
omitting support/weight
matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description
modeling_application_opportunities: and revise force models for familiar real-world systems using observations and motion evidence

title: Motion and Reference Frames
learning_target: Students will explain that motion is relative and describe an object’s motion using an appropriate frame of reference.
i_can_statements: I can explain why an object can be moving relative to one reference frame but not another.
I can identify the reference frame used in a motion description.
I can compare motion from two different points of view and explain why everyday motion is usually described relative to Earth’s surface.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating motion as absolute
switching reference frames mid-explanation
omitting what the motion is measured relative to
modeling_application_opportunities: Compare the same object from Earth

title: Speed and Velocity
learning_target: Students will distinguish between speed and velocity and use distance, time, and direction to describe motion.
i_can_statements: I can calculate average speed from distance and time.
I can distinguish instantaneous speed from average speed.
I can explain that velocity includes both speed and direction and compare examples of constant speed, constant velocity, and changing velocity.
misconceptions_failure_points: Using speed and velocity as synonyms
reporting velocity without direction
confusing instantaneous and average speed
modeling_application_opportunities: compare constant speed with constant velocity
conceptual_anchor_headings: Table 3.1 Approximate Speeds in Different Units

title: Acceleration
learning_target: Students will explain acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes and identify acceleration from motion descriptions, data, and graphs.
i_can_statements: I can calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.
I can explain that acceleration can involve speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
I can identify positive, negative, or zero acceleration from a motion situation and interpret simple motion graphs and connect them to velocity or acceleration.
misconceptions_failure_points: Defining acceleration only as speeding up
using sign alone to decide speeding up/slowing down
confusing velocity with acceleration
modeling_application_opportunities: connect changes in speed or direction to acceleration

title: Free Fall Motion
learning_target: Students will describe free fall as motion under the influence of gravity alone and use simple free-fall relationships to determine speed or distance fallen.
i_can_statements: I can explain why objects in free fall accelerate at the same rate when air resistance is ignored.
I can use $g \approx 10\text{ m/s}^2$ to determine speed gained during free fall.
I can use free-fall patterns to compare distance fallen during different time intervals and distinguish free fall from falling with significant air resistance.
misconceptions_failure_points: Believing heavier objects fall faster in ideal free fall
treating any falling object as free fall
confusing $g$ with speed
modeling_application_opportunities: Compare ideal free fall with falling through air
predict speed and distance patterns over time

title: Velocity Vectors and Motion Modeling
learning_target: Students will use velocity vectors, motion diagrams, and simple graphs to model and explain the motion of objects.
i_can_statements: I can represent velocity with arrows that show both speed and direction.
I can compare velocity vectors to determine whether an object’s velocity is changing.
I can connect motion diagrams, data tables, and graphs to written descriptions of motion and critique an incorrect motion model and revise it using evidence.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating vector direction as optional
matching graph height to physical height
failing to distinguish position
velocity
and acceleration representations
modeling_application_opportunities: Build and critique multi-representation models of an object’s motion

title: Force and Acceleration
learning_target: Students will explain how net force and mass determine acceleration and use Newton’s Second Law to analyze changes in motion.
i_can_statements: I can explain that force causes acceleration, not just motion.
I can describe how increasing net force affects acceleration.
I can describe how increasing mass affects acceleration and use Newton’s Second Law to calculate force, mass, or acceleration in simple situations.
misconceptions_failure_points: Saying force causes motion rather than acceleration
assuming equal force gives equal acceleration for different masses
using individual force instead of net force
modeling_application_opportunities: Compare how changing force or mass changes acceleration

title: Friction and Real-World Forces
learning_target: Students will explain how friction, mass, and weight affect real-world motion.
i_can_statements: I can explain friction as a force that opposes motion or attempted motion.
I can distinguish static friction from sliding friction.
I can explain why an object can remain at rest even when pushed and distinguish mass from weight.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating friction as always equal to the applied force
confusing mass and weight
assuming friction only exists during motion
modeling_application_opportunities: compare conditions that change frictional effects

title: Free Fall and Nonfree Fall
learning_target: Students will distinguish free fall from nonfree fall and explain how air resistance affects falling motion.
i_can_statements: I can explain that free fall means gravity is the only significant force acting.
I can explain why objects in free fall accelerate at $g$ when air resistance is ignored.
I can explain why falling through air can produce acceleration less than $g$ and describe terminal speed as constant speed reached when air resistance balances weight.
misconceptions_failure_points: Calling terminal speed zero acceleration because gravity stops
assuming air resistance is constant
confusing mass and weight effects
modeling_application_opportunities: Compare objects falling in vacuum-like and air-resistance conditions
explain terminal speed from balanced forces
conceptual_anchor_headings: When Acceleration Is Less Thang—Nonfree Fall
4.6 When Acceleration Is Less Than g —Nonfree Fall

title: Newton’s Third Law and Interactions
learning_target: Students will identify force interactions and explain Newton’s Third Law using action-reaction pairs that act on different objects.
i_can_statements: I can explain that forces occur as interactions between objects.
I can identify the action and reaction forces in common situations.
I can explain why action-reaction forces are equal in strength and opposite in direction and explain why action-reaction forces do not cancel when they act on different objects.
representations: paired force arrows on different objects
misconceptions_failure_points: Pairing two forces on the same object
saying the larger object exerts the larger third-law force
claiming action-reaction forces cancel each other
modeling_application_opportunities: and contact interactions by identifying the two objects
conceptual_anchor_headings: Action and Reaction on Different Masses
5.3 Action and Reaction on Different Masses

title: Projectile Motion
learning_target: Students will model projectile motion by separating horizontal and vertical components of motion.
i_can_statements: I can define a projectile as an object moving under the influence of gravity after being launched.
I can explain why horizontal motion remains constant when air resistance is ignored.
I can explain why vertical motion accelerates downward due to gravity and describe projectile motion as the combination of horizontal constant velocity and vertical accelerated motion.
misconceptions_failure_points: Assuming horizontal force is required after launch
mixing horizontal and vertical motion
assuming gravity changes horizontal velocity when air resistance is ignored
modeling_application_opportunities: Model launched objects by separating horizontal constant-velocity motion from vertical accelerated motion

title: Momentum and Impulse
learning_target: Students will explain momentum as mass in motion and use impulse to describe how forces change momentum.
i_can_statements: I can define momentum as a quantity that depends on mass and velocity.
I can explain why a large mass, high speed, or both can produce large momentum.
I can explain impulse as force acting over a time interval and connect impulse to change in momentum.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating momentum as the same as force
ignoring direction
assuming a short large force and long small force cannot have the same impulse
modeling_application_opportunities: and collision situations by relating force-time effects to momentum change
conceptual_anchor_headings: Case 2: Decreasing Momentum Over a Long Time
Case 3: Decreasing Momentum Over a Short Time

title: Conservation of Momentum
learning_target: Students will use conservation of momentum to analyze collisions, explosions, recoil, and interacting systems.
i_can_statements: I can explain what it means for momentum to be conserved.
I can identify the system being analyzed in a momentum situation.
I can distinguish internal forces from external forces and explain why momentum is conserved in both elastic and inelastic collisions when no net external impulse acts.
misconceptions_failure_points: Conserving each object’s momentum instead of system momentum
ignoring external impulse
confusing elastic with momentum-conserving
modeling_application_opportunities: and recoil by defining the system and comparing total momentum before and after

title: Work and Energy
learning_target: Students will explain work as energy transfer and distinguish kinetic energy, potential energy, mechanical energy, and power.
i_can_statements: I can determine whether a force does work on an object.
I can explain that work requires force and motion in the direction of the force.
I can distinguish kinetic energy from potential energy and calculate simple work, power, gravitational potential energy, and kinetic energy.
misconceptions_failure_points: Assuming any applied force does work
confusing power with energy
treating kinetic and potential energy as substances
modeling_application_opportunities: Compare work and power in lifting/moving situations
connect motion and position to stored or kinetic energy

title: Conservation of Energy
learning_target: Students will apply the work-energy theorem and conservation of energy to explain motion, stopping distance, energy transformations, and mechanical systems.
i_can_statements: I can explain that work changes energy.
I can use the work-energy theorem to connect net work and change in kinetic energy.
I can explain how potential energy transforms into kinetic energy and thermal energy and explain why energy is conserved even when mechanical energy seems to “disappear.”
misconceptions_failure_points: Saying energy disappears when friction acts
treating conservation as constant kinetic energy
overlooking thermal transfer
modeling_application_opportunities: and mechanical systems through energy transfer and transformation

title: Energy in Society
learning_target: Students will evaluate energy sources, energy transformations, efficiency, and real-world energy decisions using conservation of energy.
i_can_statements: I can explain that energy is not created or destroyed but can be transferred or transformed.
I can distinguish energy source, energy carrier, and energy transformation.
I can explain why useful energy often becomes thermal energy and compare energy sources using evidence such as availability, efficiency, environmental impact, and reliability.
misconceptions_failure_points: Calling electricity an energy source in every context
treating efficiency as energy conservation failure
comparing energy choices with one criterion only
modeling_application_opportunities: Evaluate real-world energy systems using multiple evidence criteria while preserving conservation of energy

title: Vibrations and Wave Properties
learning_target: Students will describe vibrations and waves using amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, and wave speed.
i_can_statements: I can explain that a vibration is a repeated back-and-forth motion.
I can describe a wave as a disturbance that transfers energy.
I can identify amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, crest, trough, compression, and rarefaction and distinguish transverse waves from longitudinal waves.
misconceptions_failure_points: Thinking matter travels with the wave
confusing amplitude with frequency
mixing wavelength and wave speed
modeling_application_opportunities: connect measurable wave features to energy transfer

title: Wave Interactions
learning_target: Students will explain how waves interact through interference, standing waves, and the Doppler effect.
i_can_statements: I can explain constructive and destructive interference.
I can interpret simple wave-superposition diagrams.
I can describe how standing waves form and explain the Doppler effect as a change in observed frequency caused by relative motion.
misconceptions_failure_points: Adding waves without considering displacement sign
treating standing waves as motionless matter
attributing Doppler shift to actual source frequency change

title: Nature of Sound
learning_target: Students will explain sound as a longitudinal mechanical wave that requires a medium and transfers energy through vibrating particles.
i_can_statements: I can explain that sound begins with a vibrating source.
I can describe sound as compressions and rarefactions traveling through a medium.
I can explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum and compare how sound travels through solids, liquids, and gases.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating sound as particles traveling from source to listener
claiming sound travels through vacuum
assuming denser always means slower
modeling_application_opportunities: Use vibrating-source and medium models to explain sound transmission through solids

title: Reflection, Refraction, and Resonance
learning_target: Students will explain how sound reflects, refracts, and causes resonance in real-world situations.
i_can_statements: I can explain echoes as reflected sound waves.
I can explain why sound can bend when wave speed changes in different conditions.
I can describe forced vibration and define natural frequency.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating resonance as any loud sound
confusing reflection with refraction
assuming bending occurs without a speed change
modeling_application_opportunities: and forced vibration using wave behavior

title: Sound Interference and Beats
learning_target: Students will analyze sound interference and beats using wave superposition and frequency differences.
i_can_statements: I can explain how two sound waves can combine constructively or destructively.
I can describe how noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference.
I can explain beats as alternating loud and soft sound caused by close frequencies and use beat frequency to compare two sound sources.
misconceptions_failure_points: Confusing beats with amplitude modulation from one source
subtracting frequencies without magnitude
treating destructive interference as permanent energy loss

title: Nature of Light
learning_target: Students will explain light as electromagnetic radiation and describe how light travels, interacts with matter, forms shadows, and allows vision.
i_can_statements: I can explain that light is an electromagnetic wave.
I can describe the relationship between wavelength, frequency, and wave speed.
I can identify visible light as one part of the electromagnetic spectrum and distinguish transparent, translucent, and opaque materials.
misconceptions_failure_points: Thinking light needs a material medium
treating color order as speed order in vacuum
confusing transparent and translucent
modeling_application_opportunities: and the place of visible light in the electromagnetic spectrum

title: Reflection and Mirrors
learning_target: Students will use the law of reflection to explain reflected light, plane mirror images, diffuse reflection, and basic mirror behavior.
i_can_statements: I can define reflection as light bouncing from a surface.
I can identify the incident ray, reflected ray, normal line, angle of incidence, and angle of reflection.
I can apply the law of reflection to ray diagrams and explain why smooth surfaces make clear images and rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection.
misconceptions_failure_points: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal
treating diffuse reflection as no reflection
placing virtual images on the mirror surface
modeling_application_opportunities: Use ray models to predict reflection and explain clear versus diffuse images

title: Refraction and Total Internal Reflection
learning_target: Students will explain refraction as bending caused by changes in light speed and use this idea to analyze optical illusions, dispersion, rainbows, and total internal reflection.
i_can_statements: I can explain that light bends when it changes speed entering a different medium at an angle.
I can predict whether light bends toward or away from the normal.
I can explain why objects can appear shifted or bent in water and explain dispersion as separation of colors caused by different amounts of refraction.
misconceptions_failure_points: Saying light bends because it “chooses” a path
reversing toward/away from normal
applying total internal reflection in the wrong direction

title: Lenses and Optical Systems
learning_target: Students will use ray diagrams and conceptual lens models to explain how lenses form images.
i_can_statements: I can distinguish converging lenses from diverging lenses.
I can draw simple ray diagrams for lenses.
I can identify focal point, focal length, object distance, image distance, and magnification and distinguish real and virtual images formed by lenses.
misconceptions_failure_points: Assuming every converging lens makes a real image
confusing focal point with image position
inconsistent sign/diagram interpretation
modeling_application_opportunities: Use ray diagrams and lens relationships to explain image type

title: Optical Applications
learning_target: Students will apply reflection, refraction, lenses, and light-wave ideas to optical devices, vision, color effects, and real-world design problems.
i_can_statements: I can explain how optical devices use reflection, refraction, or lenses.
I can describe how the eye focuses light and why corrective lenses are useful.
I can explain how optical fibers guide light and analyze real-world phenomena such as mirages, rainbows, glare, shadows, and image formation.
misconceptions_failure_points: Using one optical principle to explain a multi-part device
confusing image formation with simple reflection
ignoring energy/light-path constraints

title: Electric Charge and Forces
learning_target: Students will explain electric charge, electric force, conservation of charge, conductors, insulators, and common charging processes.
i_can_statements: I can describe positive charge, negative charge, and neutral objects.
I can explain that like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
I can explain conservation of charge during charging interactions and distinguish conductors from insulators.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating neutral as no charges
saying charge is created during rubbing
confusing polarization with net charging
modeling_application_opportunities: Explain attraction/repulsion and charging by contact
and induction using conservation of charge

title: Electric Potential and Current
learning_target: Students will explain voltage as electric potential difference and current as the rate of charge flow in a complete circuit.
i_can_statements: I can explain electric potential energy in terms of separated charges.
I can describe voltage as energy per charge.
I can explain that current is the flow of electric charge and explain why a sustained current requires a voltage source and a complete path.
misconceptions_failure_points: Calling voltage “amount of current”
thinking current is used up
omitting the complete path or source
modeling_application_opportunities: Model how a voltage source and complete conducting path produce sustained charge flow
conceptual_anchor_headings: Flow of Charge and Electric Current
Flow of Charge and Electric Current

title: Resistance and Ohm’s Law
learning_target: Students will use Ohm’s Law to explain how voltage, current, and resistance are related in simple circuits.
i_can_statements: I can define electrical resistance as opposition to charge flow.
I can explain how wire length, thickness, material, and temperature affect resistance.
I can use Ohm’s Law to calculate voltage, current, or resistance and predict how changing voltage affects current when resistance is constant.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating resistance as current
assuming current stays fixed when voltage changes
ignoring material/geometry effects
modeling_application_opportunities: use data or graphs to relate voltage
conceptual_anchor_headings: Table 23.1 Effects of Electric Currents on the Body

title: Power and Electrical Energy
learning_target: Students will explain electric power and electrical energy use in devices, homes, and energy systems.
i_can_statements: I can define electric power as the rate at which electrical energy is transferred.
I can calculate power using voltage and current.
I can calculate electrical energy use from power and time and compare energy use of household devices.
misconceptions_failure_points: Confusing power with energy
comparing devices without time
treating higher power as automatically less efficient
conceptual_anchor_headings: Speed and Source of Electrons in a Circuit
Speed and Source of Electrons in a Circuit

title: Complex Electric Circuits
learning_target: Students will analyze series, parallel, and mixed circuits by tracing current paths, comparing voltage drops, and explaining how circuit changes affect brightness, current, resistance, and safety.
i_can_statements: I can distinguish series circuits from parallel circuits.
I can explain why a complete circuit is required for steady current.
I can trace current paths through simple and branched circuits and compare voltage and current in series and parallel circuits.
misconceptions_failure_points: Thinking current chooses only one parallel branch
treating voltage/current rules as identical for series and parallel
failing to distinguish open and short circuits
modeling_application_opportunities: connect design choices to brightness and safety

title: Magnetism and Magnetic Fields
learning_target: Students will explain magnetic poles, magnetic fields, and magnetic domains using field models and everyday magnetic interactions.
i_can_statements: I can explain that magnets have north and south poles.
I can describe how like magnetic poles repel and unlike magnetic poles attract.
I can explain that magnetic field lines show the direction and relative strength of a magnetic field and explain why magnetic poles are not isolated as single north or south poles.
misconceptions_failure_points: Treating field lines as physical strings
assuming isolated magnetic poles are ordinary
confusing field direction with object motion
modeling_application_opportunities: and domain models to explain attraction

title: Electricity and Magnetism
learning_target: Students will explain how electric current produces magnetic fields and how changing electric and magnetic fields are connected.
i_can_statements: I can explain that moving electric charges create magnetic fields.
I can describe the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.
I can explain how a compass can detect a magnetic field produced by current and compare magnetic fields around a straight wire, loop, and coil.
misconceptions_failure_points: Thinking only permanent magnets make magnetic fields
reversing current without considering field reversal
confusing electric and magnetic field models
modeling_application_opportunities: Investigate and compare magnetic fields produced by straight wires

title: Electromagnets and Magnetic Forces
learning_target: Students will analyze electromagnets and magnetic forces on moving charges and current-carrying wires.
i_can_statements: I can explain that a current-carrying coil of wire is an electromagnet.
I can describe how increasing current or coil turns affects electromagnet strength.
I can explain how an iron core can strengthen an electromagnet and explain that moving charges can experience magnetic forces.
misconceptions_failure_points: Assuming more turns always increases strength regardless of current/core
treating magnetic force as parallel to motion
confusing field with force
modeling_application_opportunities: Analyze electromagnet strength and force interactions in coils

title: Generators and Alternating Current
learning_target: Students will explain how generators use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy and why alternating current changes direction.
i_can_statements: I can explain that electromagnetic induction can produce voltage when magnetic conditions change.
I can describe how rotating a coil in a magnetic field can induce voltage.
I can explain that a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy and explain why the output of a common generator is alternating current.
misconceptions_failure_points: Thinking a steady magnetic field automatically induces voltage
confusing motor and generator energy direction
treating AC as energy disappearing and reappearing
modeling_application_opportunities: Explain generator operation and alternating output through changing magnetic conditions and energy conversion

title: Modern Electromagnetic Systems
learning_target: Students will apply magnetism, electromagnets, magnetic forces, and electromagnetic induction to real-world technologies and systems.
i_can_statements: I can explain how electromagnetic systems use energy transformations.
I can describe how generators, motors, transformers, speakers, microphones, maglev systems, MRI, and electric meters use electromagnetism.
I can explain why energy input is required for electrical energy output and critique claims that a device produces energy from magnetism alone.
misconceptions_failure_points: Claiming magnets supply unlimited energy
ignoring energy input/output
using device labels without explaining field/current/induction mechanism
modeling_application_opportunities: Analyze modern electromagnetic technologies and critique claims about their operation or energy source
